paragraphs.source_en: The rock art representing clearly domesticated animals is more easily chronologically assessed. The archaeological record indicates domesticated cattle in the Central Sahara after 7,500 BP (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996c; Mori 2000) which is the earliest date applicable to the Pastoral engravings and paintings. An image of a domesticated cow or bull in the Yat depression in Northeastern Niger was carved on rock that had been consequently flooded in a swampy basin. The 14C dates from this layer are 7,760+330 BP (cal BP 8,661±378) and 7,840+330 BP (calBP 8,757±377) indicating the ante quem limit for the execution of the engravings (Striedter 1996). A similar situation occurs in the Algerian Tadrart in Wadi Tidounadj where the lower part of an engraving of cattle is covered with sediments from the water flow forming a terrace.

paragraphs.source_en: In the Acacus, samples consisting of small sandstone fragments painted with red and yellow ochre pigments were collected from site debris in the Lancusi rock shelter. The poorly preserved painting from which the fragments came represents animals with long shaped horns, probably cows or gazelles. They were attributed to the Pastoral style and directly dated to 6,145+70 BP (calBP 7,048±96). At A-Fozzigiart shelter an image of cattle was directly dated to 4,990+50 BP (calBP 5,758±88). Small red human figures at Tin Torha North were dated to 4,040+200 BP (calBP 4,518±273) (Ponti & Sinibaldi 2005; Mori et al. 2006). During the excavations at Uan Muhuggiag shelter in the Acacus a stratigraphic layer contained a piece of rock which had detached from the above wall as a result of a thermoclastic phenomenon.
